title: Hop Across the Stepping Stones
statement:
Stones sit along a straight stream at the positions in stones, given in strictly increasing order. The first stone is always at position 0, and a hopper starts on it.

The hopper only moves forward and must always land on a stone. Its first hop is exactly 1 unit. After a hop of k units, the next hop must be k − 1, k or k + 1 units long (and longer than 0).

Return true if the hopper can reach the last stone, otherwise false.

examples.why: Hops of 1, 2, 2, 3, 4. Each hop is within one of the previous hop.
The first hop must be exactly 1 unit, and there is no stone at position 1.
Always taking the longest hop fails: 0 → 1 → 3 → 6 leaves a speed of 3, too fast for the 7. Slowing down works: 0 → 1 → 3 → 4 → 6 → 7.

hints: Where the hopper can go next depends on two things: which stone it is on and how long its last hop was.
So the state is (stone, last hop). There are at most n different hop lengths that matter, which keeps the number of states around n².
Keep, for every stone, the set of hop lengths that can arrive there. Walk the stones left to right and push k − 1, k, k + 1 forward from each one, using a map from position to stone.

explain.intuition:
Knowing only the current stone is not enough, because the same stone can be reached fast or slow and that changes the next options. In the third example stone 6 is reachable at speed 3 (useless) and at speed 2 (works). So the state is the pair (stone, last hop length).

Once you see that, it is a reachability fill. Give every stone a set of the hop lengths that can land on it. Stone 0 starts with a "previous hop" of 0, so its only next hop is 1. Process stones from left to right; every hop length k stored on a stone sends the hopper to pos + k − 1, pos + k and pos + k + 1, and if a stone sits there, that length joins its set. The answer is whether the last stone's set is non-empty.
steps: Build a map from position to a set of hop lengths, one empty set per stone.
Put the length 0 in the set of stone 0, standing for "not moved yet", so its next hop is forced to 1.
Go through the stones in order. For every length k in its set and every step in k − 1, k, k + 1 with step > 0, if pos + step is a stone, add step to that stone's set.
Return whether the last stone's set is non-empty.
pitfalls: Tracking only which stones are reachable, without the speed. Two arrivals at the same stone with different speeds lead to different futures.
Allowing a first hop of 0 or 2. The first hop is exactly 1, which is why [0, 2] is false.
Indexing an array by position. Positions go up to about two billion; use a map from position to stone.

solutions.title: Plain depth-first search
solutions.idea: Try all three hop lengths from every stone recursively. Correct, but the same (stone, speed) pair gets explored again and again.

solutions.title: Memoized search on (stone, speed)
solutions.idea: The same DFS, but remember every (stone, last hop) pair already explored so each is expanded once.

solutions.title: Forward fill of arrival speeds
solutions.idea: Every stone keeps the set of hop lengths that can land on it. Walk the stones left to right and push each length forward.

followups: Return the fewest hops needed to reach the last stone, or -1.
Hops may also go backward. Does the forward fill still work? What would you use instead?
